gloss: A short summary of the main news items, or an operation to gather people or animals together.
examples: The morning *roundup* covers all the big stories in five minutes.
Police carried out a *roundup* of suspects before dawn.
We watched the cattle *roundup* from the fence.

gloss: The practice of changing a number to a simpler value close to it.
examples: The difference is just a *rounding* error.
*Rounding* to two decimal places is accurate enough here.
The columns don't add up because of *rounding*.

gloss: A crushing, completely one-sided defeat.
examples: The game turned into a 42-7 *rout*.
What started as a close race ended in a *rout*.
The army's *rout* at the river ended the campaign.
contrast: Many Americans say *route* as ROWT too, so *rout* (a defeat) and *route* (a road) can sound identical — only context separates them.

gloss: A vehicle built to drive over rough ground, especially one exploring another planet.
examples: The *rover* sent back the first color photos of the Martian surface.
Two *rovers* are still operating on Mars.
The lunar *rover* folded up to fit inside the lander.

gloss: An act of pressing your hand over something and moving it back and forth.
examples: She gave the dog a quick *rub* behind the ears.
A back *rub* would feel wonderful right now.
He gave the windshield one last *rub* with the cloth.

gloss: The basic unit of money in Russia.
examples: The *ruble* fell sharply against the dollar last week.
He paid two hundred *rubles* for the ticket.
All the prices in the window were listed in *rubles*.

gloss: A basic principle or first element of a subject, almost always used in the plural.
examples: He learned the *rudiments* of chess in a single weekend.
The course covers only the *rudiments* of accounting.
She picked up the *rudiments* of Spanish while traveling.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Complete collapse or destruction; in the plural, the remains of a destroyed building.
examples: The lawsuit meant financial *ruin* for the family.
We spent the afternoon walking through the *ruins* of an old abbey.
The tornado left the barn in *ruins*.

gloss: A Cuban ballroom dance with a strong rhythm, or the music written for it.
examples: They took lessons so they could dance the *rumba* at the wedding.
The band closed the set with a slow *rumba*.
She won the competition with a flawless *rumba*.

gloss: A long, low, rolling sound.
examples: We heard the distant *rumble* of thunder over the hills.
The *rumble* of trucks on the highway kept me awake.
A low *rumble* came from his empty stomach.

gloss: A card game in which players collect matching sets and runs of cards.
examples: We played *rummy* at the kitchen table until midnight.
My grandmother taught me *rummy* when I was six.
He's much better at *rummy* than at poker.

gloss: The back end of an animal, or the cut of meat taken from it.
examples: The horse's *rump* was covered with a wool blanket.
She bought a *rump* roast for Sunday dinner.
Each calf had a brand on its *rump*.

gloss: Someone, especially a teenager, who has left home without permission.
examples: The shelter takes in teenage *runaways*.
Police found the *runaway* at a bus station in Denver.
She was a *runaway* at sixteen and never went back.

gloss: A letter of an ancient Germanic alphabet, usually carved into stone or wood.
examples: The gravestone was covered in *runes*.
He had a *rune* tattooed on his forearm.
Scholars still argue about what these *runes* mean.

gloss: One of the horizontal bars of a ladder that you put your foot on.
examples: The bottom *rung* of the ladder was rotten.
She climbed two more *rungs* and stopped.
He started on the lowest *rung* of the company.
contrast: *Rung* is also the past participle of *ring* ("the bell has rung") — same spelling, completely unrelated meaning.

gloss: The period of time leading up to an important event.
examples: Spending always rises in the *run-up* to Christmas.
The polls tightened during the *run-up* to the election.
There were three weeks of rehearsals in the *run-up* to opening night.

gloss: A break or tear in something, or a serious break in a relationship.
examples: A *rupture* in the pipeline spilled thousands of gallons of oil.
The argument caused a lasting *rupture* between the two brothers.
Surgeons repaired the *rupture* in the artery.

gloss: A clever trick used to fool someone.
examples: The phone call was a *ruse* to get her out of the house.
They saw through his *ruse* almost immediately.
The whole party turned out to be an elaborate *ruse*.

gloss: A soft sound made by light things brushing against each other.
examples: There was a *rustle* in the bushes behind us.
She heard the *rustle* of paper from the next room.
A faint *rustle* of leaves was the only sound.

gloss: A large round root vegetable with firm yellow flesh.
examples: She mashed the *rutabaga* with butter and pepper.
*Rutabagas* keep all winter in a cold cellar.
The stew had carrots, potatoes, and *rutabaga*.
contrast: What Americans call a *rutabaga*, the British call a *swede* — the same vegetable.

gloss: A sword with a curved blade, also used as one of the three fencing weapons.
examples: The officer's *saber* hung above the fireplace.
She competes in *saber* at the national level.
Two crossed *sabers* were mounted on the wall.
contrast: American *saber*, British *sabre* — same word, different spelling.

gloss: Someone who deliberately damages equipment or plans in order to stop them working.
examples: A *saboteur* had cut the power lines to the plant.
They suspected there were *saboteurs* inside the company.
The general feared *saboteurs* more than an open attack.

gloss: An artificial sweetener used in place of sugar.
examples: The diet soda is sweetened with *saccharin*.
She keeps a little box of *saccharin* tablets in her purse.
Some people say *saccharin* leaves a bitter aftertaste.
contrast: *Saccharin* (no final e) is the sweetener; *saccharine* is an adjective meaning sickeningly sentimental.

gloss: A formal Christian religious ceremony such as baptism or marriage.
examples: Baptism is the first of the seven *sacraments*.
The priest administered the last *sacrament*.
Marriage is considered a *sacrament* in the Catholic Church.

gloss: A bag fastened to the side of a saddle, bicycle, or motorcycle.
examples: He stuffed the map into his *saddlebag*.
Both *saddlebags* were packed with camping gear.
The motorcycle came with leather *saddlebags*.

gloss: Pleasure taken in causing pain or suffering to others.
examples: There was real *sadism* in the way he mocked her.
Critics attacked the film for its casual *sadism*.
*Sadism* has no place in a classroom.

gloss: Someone who enjoys causing pain or suffering to others.
examples: Only a *sadist* would find that funny.
The coach was a *sadist* about conditioning drills.
She described her old boss as a petty *sadist*.

gloss: A long story covering many years, or a long and complicated series of events.
examples: The whole *saga* took three years to resolve.
She's writing a family *saga* set in Chicago.
It's a *saga* I'd rather forget.

gloss: A gray-green desert shrub that covers much of the American West.
examples: Nothing grew out there but *sagebrush* and rock.
The smell of *sagebrush* came through the open window.
*Sagebrush* covers thousands of square miles of Nevada.

gloss: A giant branching cactus that grows in the deserts of the American Southwest.
examples: A hundred-year-old *saguaro* stood beside the road.
*Saguaros* can grow forty feet tall.
It is illegal to cut down a *saguaro* in Arizona.
contrast: The *gu* is pronounced like a *w*: suh-WAH-roh, not sag-YOO-ar-oh.

gloss: Skill in persuading people to buy things.
examples: It took real *salesmanship* to close that deal.
His *salesmanship* was better than his product.
The training focused on *salesmanship* and follow-up calls.

gloss: A type of bacteria found in food that causes serious food poisoning.
examples: Dozens of people got sick from *salmonella* in the chicken.
The plant shut down after a *salmonella* outbreak.
Raw eggs can carry *salmonella*.

gloss: A greeting, especially the opening words of a letter or email.
examples: Begin the letter with a formal *salutation*.
"Dear Sir" is an old-fashioned *salutation*.
He skipped the *salutation* and got straight to business.

gloss: The rescue of property from wreckage or loss, or the goods rescued that way.
examples: The *salvage* operation lasted three weeks.
He buys parts at a *salvage* yard outside town.
Most of the *salvage* from the wreck turned out to be worthless.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A soothing ointment put on sore or injured skin.
examples: She rubbed a little *salve* on the burn.
The pharmacy sells a *salve* for chapped lips.
His apology was a *salve* to her wounded pride.

gloss: A fast Brazilian dance, or the music played for it.
examples: They danced the *samba* until three in the morning.
A *samba* band led the parade down the avenue.
She teaches *samba* on Tuesday nights.

gloss: A fried triangular pastry filled with spiced vegetables or meat.
examples: We ordered *samosas* to start.
The *samosa* was still too hot to eat.
She makes *samosas* with potato and peas.

gloss: A selection of small portions of different things offered so you can try each one.
examples: We split the appetizer *sampler*.
The bakery sells a cookie *sampler* every December.
The label put out a free *sampler* of new bands.

gloss: The practice of choosing a small group or amount to represent a much larger whole.
examples: Random *sampling* is what keeps the survey honest.
Water *sampling* is done twice a month at each site.
The study's *sampling* method has been questioned.

gloss: A fragrant tropical wood, or the scent taken from it.
examples: The soap smells faintly of *sandalwood*.
He carved the little box out of *sandalwood*.
*Sandalwood* oil is expensive and easy to fake.

gloss: A soft rock formed from pressed sand, often used for building.
examples: The cliffs above the river are red *sandstone*.
The old church is built of local *sandstone*.
Water has carved deep channels through the *sandstone*.

gloss: The use of remarks that mean the opposite of what they say, in order to mock someone.
examples: I couldn't tell whether he was serious or using *sarcasm*.
Her voice was heavy with *sarcasm*.
*Sarcasm* doesn't come across well in a text message.

gloss: A long piece of cloth wrapped around the body, worn by women in South Asia.
examples: She wore a red silk *sari* to the wedding.
The shop sells *saris* and gold jewelry.
He watched her fold the *sari* carefully.

gloss: A long strip of cloth wrapped around the waist and worn like a skirt.
examples: She pulled a *sarong* on over her swimsuit.
The hotel gift shop sells *sarongs* in every color.
He wore a cotton *sarong* around the house all summer.

gloss: A wide band of cloth worn around the waist or over one shoulder.
examples: The mayor wore a ceremonial *sash*.
Her dress had a pale blue *sash* at the waist.
The winners were given *sashes* and flowers.

gloss: Thin slices of raw fish served on their own, without rice.
examples: He ordered *sashimi* instead of sushi.
The tuna *sashimi* was the best thing on the table.
*Sashimi* should be eaten the day it's cut.
contrast: *Sashimi* is raw fish alone; *sushi* refers to the vinegared rice, with or without fish.

gloss: Rude or cheeky talk directed at someone in authority.
examples: Don't give me any *sass*, young man.
That kid has plenty of *sass* for a six-year-old.
She took no *sass* from anybody on the crew.

gloss: A writer or performer who mocks people and institutions to expose their faults.
examples: He made his name as a political *satirist*.
Two *satirists* were arrested over the cartoon.
The magazine hired a *satirist* to write the back page.

gloss: The state of being completely filled or soaked, or the intensity of a color.
examples: The market for these apps has reached *saturation*.
Turn down the *saturation* a little on that photo.
Rain kept falling well past the point of soil *saturation*.

gloss: Shredded cabbage that has been salted and left to ferment.
examples: He put mustard and *sauerkraut* on his hot dog.
The recipe calls for a cup of drained *sauerkraut*.
Homemade *sauerkraut* takes about three weeks.

gloss: The fine powder of wood produced by sawing.
examples: The whole floor was covered in *sawdust*.
He swept the *sawdust* into a pile by the door.
The shop smelled of *sawdust* and varnish.

gloss: A wooden or metal frame used to hold boards while you cut them.
examples: He laid the door across two *sawhorses*.
The *sawhorse* wobbled under the weight of the beam.
We used *sawhorses* to block off the driveway.

gloss: A factory where logs are cut into boards.
examples: The town grew up around the *sawmill*.
His father worked at the *sawmill* for thirty years.
Two *sawmills* closed last winter.

gloss: An informal word for a saxophone.
examples: He plays *sax* in a jazz trio downtown.
She brought her *sax* to the rehearsal.
The tune opens with a lonely *sax*.

gloss: A musician who plays the saxophone.
examples: The *saxophonist* took a long solo in the second set.
She's the best *saxophonist* in the school band.
Two *saxophonists* joined the group last year.

gloss: The hard crust that forms over a healing wound.
examples: Don't pick at that *scab* or it will scar.
The *scab* fell off after about a week.
His knees were covered in *scabs* from the fall.

gloss: A contagious skin disease caused by tiny mites that burrow under the skin.
examples: An outbreak of *scabies* closed the dorm for a week.
*Scabies* is treated with a prescription cream.
She caught *scabies* at summer camp.

gloss: The ability of a system or business to grow much larger without breaking down.
examples: The investors asked about *scalability* first.
The design has real *scalability* problems.
*Scalability* matters more here than raw speed.

gloss: A small, very sharp knife used by surgeons.
examples: The surgeon reached for a *scalpel*.
Two *scalpels* were missing from the tray.
He trimmed the drawing with a *scalpel*.

gloss: Shrimp cooked in garlic butter, usually served over pasta or with bread.
examples: I ordered the shrimp *scampi*.
Her *scampi* recipe uses a whole head of garlic.
The *scampi* came with a side of linguine.

gloss: Someone who is blamed for the mistakes of other people.
examples: The manager became the *scapegoat* for a bad season.
They needed a *scapegoat*, and he was convenient.
Immigrants are often made *scapegoats* in hard times.

gloss: A shortage of something that people need.
examples: There's a real *scarcity* of affordable housing in the city.
The drought caused a *scarcity* of feed for cattle.
Wartime *scarcities* forced families to ration everything.

gloss: A sudden feeling of fear, or a public alarm about some danger.
examples: That noise gave me a real *scare*.
He had a health *scare* last spring but he's fine now.
A bomb *scare* emptied the building at noon.

gloss: An animal that feeds on dead flesh or waste, or a person who searches through discarded things.
examples: Vultures and hyenas are *scavengers*.
The kids spent the afternoon on a *scavenger* hunt.
*Scavengers* had already picked through the dumpster.

gloss: An ornamental rod carried by a king or queen as a symbol of power.
examples: The queen held the *scepter* in her right hand.
A crown and *scepter* lay on the velvet cushion.
The museum displays two jeweled *scepters*.
contrast: American *scepter*, British *sceptre*; the *sc* is said like a plain *s*.

gloss: The work of arranging when things will happen.
examples: A *scheduling* conflict kept her out of the meeting.
The software handles all the *scheduling* automatically.
Poor *scheduling* cost the crew two full days.
contrast: Americans say SKEJ-ool; the British say SHED-yool.

gloss: A simplified drawing showing how the parts of a system connect.
examples: He pulled up the wiring *schematic* on his laptop.
The *schematics* were locked in a safe.
Follow the *schematic* exactly or nothing will work.

gloss: A plan, especially a clever or dishonest one.
examples: The whole thing was a *scheme* to avoid taxes.
He fell for a get-rich-quick *scheme*.
Their *schemes* finally caught up with them.
contrast: In American English a *scheme* usually sounds dishonest; in British English it is a neutral word for an official program.

gloss: A deep split that divides a church, party, or other group into opposing sides.
examples: A *schism* split the congregation in two.
The vote caused a lasting *schism* in the party.
Old *schisms* resurfaced at the convention.
contrast: The *sch* is said /sk/: SKIZ-uhm, not SHIZ-uhm.

gloss: A boy who goes to school.
examples: He grinned like a *schoolboy* caught telling a joke.
A group of *schoolboys* waited at the bus stop.
She still remembers him as a skinny *schoolboy*.

gloss: A child who attends school.
examples: Every American *schoolchild* learns that story.
Thousands of *schoolchildren* visit the museum each year.
The bus was packed with *schoolchildren*.

gloss: A girl who goes to school.
examples: She blushed like a *schoolgirl*.
Two *schoolgirls* were selling cookies outside the store.
The photo shows her as a *schoolgirl* in uniform.

gloss: Education received at school.
examples: He had only six years of *schooling*.
Her *schooling* was interrupted by the war.
*Schooling* is free here through twelfth grade.

gloss: The open area beside a school where children play.
examples: They met in the *schoolyard* after class.
The argument started in the *schoolyard*.
Snow covered the empty *schoolyard*.

gloss: A sailing ship with two or more masts and fore-and-aft sails.
examples: A wooden *schooner* was moored at the end of the pier.
They restored the old *schooner* over five years.
Two *schooners* raced up the coast.

gloss: The weak, neutral vowel sound heard in the first syllable of *about*.
examples: The last syllable is reduced to a *schwa*.
English is full of *schwas* in unstressed syllables.
The symbol for the *schwa* is an upside-down e.

gloss: Pain running down the back of the leg, caused by pressure on the sciatic nerve.
examples: Her *sciatica* flares up when she sits too long.
He's been off work with *sciatica* since March.
Stretching helps the *sciatica* a little.

gloss: A small, slightly sweet baked cake, often eaten with coffee or tea.
examples: She had a blueberry *scone* with her latte.
The bakery puts out fresh *scones* every morning.
This *scone* is a little dry.
contrast: Two accepted pronunciations: SKOHN (usual in the US) and SKAHN — people argue about which is correct.

gloss: A player who scores points or goals, or the person who keeps the score.
examples: She's the team's leading *scorer* this season.
Both *scorers* came off the bench in the fourth quarter.
The *scorer* wrote down every basket.
